approved: Introduced amendments to the National Measurement Act, in operation since July 2010 to oversee an estimated $400 billion a year in measurement-based trade, giving inspectors discretion to allow a 28-day grace period for traders to fix minor non-compliance rather than immediately pulling goods or instruments from use.

Supported the bill correcting deficiencies in the national trade measurement system nearly three years after its introduction, but criticised the government for stonewalling a 2011 Senate estimates question about problems with the rollout, and noted 150 of 184 questions from the most recent estimates round remain unanswered after around three months.

Supported technical amendments to the National Measurement Act, including a new 28-day period for traders to fix minor compliance issues, noted the 2009 COAG reform unified eight state trade measurement systems into one covering $4 billion of trade a year, and highlighted that the National Measurement Institute houses Australia's three atomic clocks and its reference kilogram.

Backed the National Measurement Amendment Bill's uncontroversial fixes, including letting inspectors give traders up to 28 days to fix non-compliant instruments, but cautioned that a new power letting inspectors enter public areas without first announcing themselves needs careful drafting to avoid disrupting legitimate businesses.

Summed up the National Measurement Amendment Bill as refining the national trade measurement system that replaced eight separate state systems when it began operating in July 2010, giving inspectors more flexibility to let businesses, particularly in remote communities, resolve minor compliance issues within a reasonable time frame.

The coalition supported the National Measurement Amendment Bill 2013, which clarifies measures from earlier legislation, aligns provisions with current state practices, and specifies offences such as failing to remove verification marks after repairs affecting performance.
